subject: rla
title: Grammar II: Agreement, Pronouns, Tense, Confused Words, Capitals, Apostrophes, Commas
objectives: Students will make verbs agree with their subjects, including subjects separated from the verb by phrases, indefinite pronouns such as each and everyone, and compound subjects joined by and, or, and nor.
Students will choose pronouns that agree with their antecedents in number and use the correct case (I/me, she/her, we/us) in compound subjects and objects.
Students will keep verb tense consistent within a sentence and a paragraph, using time clues to choose past, present, future, or present perfect.
Students will distinguish frequently confused words (their/there/they're, its/it's, your/you're, affect/effect, then/than) and apply rules for capitalization, apostrophes, and commas.
Students will answer GED-style editing items in which drop-down options differ by a single word, letter, capital, or punctuation mark.
teach:
Lesson overview

Week 7 focused on how sentences are built. Week 8 focuses on the small choices inside a sentence that make writing correct: verb and subject agreement, pronoun choice, verb tense, frequently confused words, capital letters, apostrophes, and commas. On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, these skills appear mostly as drop-down menus inside short workplace and community documents such as emails, notices, and letters. The options often differ by only one letter or one punctuation mark, so learners must slow down and test each choice against a rule.

Objectives

  • Make subjects and verbs agree, even when a phrase separates them.
  • Choose pronouns that agree in number and use the correct case.
  • Keep verb tense consistent with the time clues in a passage.
  • Tell apart their/there/they're, its/it's, your/you're, affect/effect, and then/than.
  • Apply core rules for capital letters, apostrophes, and commas.

Materials

  • Student Lesson (printed or on screen) and this week's Notes sheet
  • Whiteboard or shared screen; markers in two colors (one for subjects, one for verbs)
  • Copies of the warm-up note and the guided-practice notice (both below)
  • Week 8 practice items: items 1–6 (the check-in email and the water notice) are used for independent practice
  • Index cards or a shared document for the exit ticket

60-minute timing plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5“Spot five”: find and fix five errors in a short note
Direct instruction20Agreement, pronoun case, tense consistency, confused words, capitals, apostrophes, commas; three worked examples
Guided practice15Whole-group editing of a parking notice with five choices
Independent practice15Practice items 1–6; circulate and coach
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; exit ticket; assign the week's study plan

Warm-up (5 minutes): Spot five

Display this note. Tell learners it contains exactly five errors. They work alone for three minutes, then compare with a partner.

Hi Marcus,

The new schedules is posted in the break room. Please check you're shift for next week, and let me know if their are any problems. Me and Dana will be in the office on monday.

Thanks, Lena

Answers: (1) schedules is → schedules are (plural subject); (2) you're shift → your shift (possession, not “you are”); (3) their are → there are (“there” introduces something that exists); (4) Me and Dana will be → Dana and I will be (subject case; drop “Dana and” and you would say “I will be”); (5) monday → Monday (days of the week are capitalized). A spell-checker would miss most of these, which is why the GED tests them.

Direct instruction (20 minutes): talking points

1. Subject-verb agreement

  • A singular subject takes a singular verb (The list is); a plural subject takes a plural verb (The lists are). In the present tense, the singular verb usually ends in -s.
  • Cross out the phrase in the middle. In “The box of old files is heavy,” the subject is box, not files. Phrases beginning with of, in, with, along with, as well as, and including never change the subject.
  • Each, every, everyone, everybody, someone, nobody, either, and neither (used alone) are singular: Everyone on both teams has a badge.
  • Two subjects joined by and are plural. With or or nor, the verb agrees with the closer subject: Neither the drivers nor the manager was told.
  • In sentences that begin with There is/There are, the subject comes after the verb: There are two problems.
  • A company, team, or department named as one unit is singular: The committee meets on Tuesdays.

2. Pronouns: agreement and case

  • A pronoun must agree in number with its antecedent, the word it replaces: The employees picked up their checks. The company changed its policy.
  • Subject case (I, he, she, we, they, who) is used for the doer of an action. Object case (me, him, her, us, them, whom) is used after a verb or a preposition.
  • Drop-the-partner test: In “Ms. Ruiz called Tanya and (I/me),” cover “Tanya and.” “Ms. Ruiz called me” sounds right, so the answer is me.
  • Between is a preposition, so it is always between you and me, never between you and I.

3. Verb tense consistency

  • Pick the tense that matches the time clues (yesterday, last year, now, next week, since) and stay in it unless the time actually changes.
  • Shifting without a reason is an error: Last week I called the office and ask for a refund should be asked.
  • Use the present perfect (has/have + past participle) for an action that started in the past and continues or matters now, often with since or for: She has worked here since 2019.

4. Frequently confused words

WordMeaning or jobTest
their / there / they'rebelonging to them / a place or “there is” / they areCan you say “they are”? Then they're.
its / it'sbelonging to it / it is or it hasCan you say “it is”? Then it's. Otherwise its.
your / you'rebelonging to you / you areCan you say “you are”?
affect / effectusually a verb (to influence) / usually a noun (a result)After a, an, the, or an adjective, use effect.
then / thantime or next step / comparisonMore than, less than, rather than always use than.

5. Capitalization

  • Capitalize names of specific people, places, organizations, streets, days, months, and holidays: Juniper Street, Tuesday, March, Labor Day.
  • Do not capitalize seasons (fall, spring), general words (the street, a hospital), or most school subjects (math, history). Languages are capitalized (English, Spanish).
  • Capitalize a title right before a name (Doctor Lee) but not a title used alone (the doctor).

6. Apostrophes

  • Possession, one owner: add 's (the manager's desk). Plural owners ending in -s: add only the apostrophe (the managers' meeting). Plurals not ending in -s add 's (the children's room).
  • Contractions: the apostrophe replaces missing letters (don't, it's, they're).
  • Never use an apostrophe to make a word plural: three volunteers, not three volunteer's. Possessive pronouns never take one: its, yours, theirs, hers.

7. Commas

  • After an introductory clause or long phrase: When the meeting ends, please lock the door.
  • Between items in a series of three or more: pens, paper, and tape.
  • Before and, but, or, so when they join two complete sentences: The store opened, but the lights were off.
  • Around extra (nonessential) information: Our supervisor, Dana Whitfield, will be on site. Use a pair of commas, not just one.
  • No comma between a subject and its verb, or between a verb and its object.

Worked examples

Example 1 (agreement with a phrase in the middle). Choose the verb: “The list of approved vendors (is / are) posted on the shared drive.”

Step 1. Find the verb choices: is or are.

Step 2. Cross out the prepositional phrase: “The list [of approved vendors] (is / are) posted.” On the board, draw a line through the bracketed phrase.

Step 3. The subject is list, which is singular.

Step 4. A singular subject takes a singular verb: “The list of approved vendors is posted.”

Trap: the plural vendors sits next to the verb, so “vendors are” sounds right.

Example 2 (pronoun case in a compound). Choose: “The supervisor asked Tanya and (I / me) to cover the Saturday shift.”

Step 1. Drop the partner: “The supervisor asked (I / me) to cover.”

Step 2. “Asked me” sounds right; “asked I” does not.

Step 3. The pronoun receives the action of asked, so it needs object case: “asked Tanya and me.”

Contrast: “Tanya and (I / me) covered the shift.” Drop the partner: “I covered.” Here the pronoun is a subject, so I is correct.

Example 3 (a GED-style menu where only punctuation differs). “[    ▾] the store will close early on Friday.” Options: (a) Because the floors are being refinished, (b) Because the floors are being refinished (c) Because, the floors are being refinished, (d) Because the floors, are being refinished,

Step 1. Only the commas change, so this is a comma question.

Step 2. The words form an introductory clause (it has a subject, floors, and a verb, are being refinished) that comes before the main clause. An introductory clause is followed by a comma, so (b) is wrong.

Step 3. No comma goes right after Because, because that splits the clause from the word that introduces it, so (c) is wrong. No comma goes between a subject and its verb, so (d) is wrong.

Answer: (a) Because the floors are being refinished, the store will close early on Friday.

In Example 1, model the cross-out with a marker on the board. Have learners physically draw the line through the phrase on their own copies; the habit transfers directly to test day.

Guided practice (15 minutes)

Display the notice. Work through each choice together. For every choice, ask a learner to name the rule before you confirm the answer.

Notice to Tenants: Parking Lot Repaving

The parking lot, along with both side driveways, (1) [is / are] closed this Friday. Last year, repaving took two days and (2) [causes / caused / will cause] very few problems. (3) [Their / There / They're] will be free parking on Oak Avenue all day. (4) [If it rains, the / If it rains the / If, it rains the] work will move to Monday. Tenants who need help moving a car should call Ms. Cho or (5) [I / me / myself].

Answers: (1) is: the subject is lot; “along with both side driveways” is a phrase that does not change the subject. (2) caused: “Last year” and the past-tense took set the time in the past. (3) There: it introduces something that exists; you cannot say “They are will be.” (4) If it rains, the: a comma follows the introductory clause If it rains, and no comma belongs after If. (5) me: it is the object of call; drop “Ms. Cho or” and you would say “call me.” Myself is used only when the subject is also I (“I did it myself”).

Checks for understanding (with expected answers)

  1. “A box of gloves (sit / sits) on the shelf.” Which verb? Expected: sits. The subject is box.
  2. Which is correct, “between you and I” or “between you and me”? Expected: between you and me, because between is a preposition and takes object case.
  3. When is its written with an apostrophe? Expected: only when it means “it is” or “it has.” The possessive its never has an apostrophe.
  4. Fix: “The Nguyen's live next door.” Expected: The Nguyens live next door. It is a plural, not a possessive.
  5. Should summer be capitalized in “We hire extra staff every summer”? Expected: No. Seasons are not capitalized.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Agreeing with the nearest noun. Learners choose “The cost of repairs are” because repairs is next to the verb. Correction: always cross out phrases that begin with a preposition, then match the verb to what is left.

“Me and him went.” This is common in speech but wrong in formal writing. Correction: drop the partner (“Me went” sounds wrong), then reorder: “He and I went.”

Using it's for possession. Learners reason that possession takes an apostrophe. Correction: possessive pronouns (his, hers, its, ours, yours, theirs) never take apostrophes. Say “it is” aloud; if it does not fit, drop the apostrophe.

Apostrophes on plurals. “We need volunteer's.” Correction: ask “Does the word own anything?” If not, no apostrophe.

Tense drift in stories. Learners begin in the past and slide into the present (“I walked in and the manager says...”). Correction: underline every verb in the paragraph and check that each one matches the time clues.

Too many commas. Learners put a comma at every pause. Correction: name the rule or leave the comma out.

Differentiation

Support: Have learners color subjects in one color and verbs in another before choosing. Give them a card listing the quick tests. Assign one rule per day in the study plan rather than all seven at once.

Stretch: Introduce who vs. whom (use the he/him test: “whom” matches “him”), collective nouns used as units, and either/or and neither/nor agreement. Ask learners to write their own GED-style menu item with four options that differ only by punctuation, then trade with a partner.

How this shows up on the GED

  • Language skills are tested mostly with drop-down menus placed inside a passage. The passages are usually practical documents: emails, letters, memos, notices, and short articles.
  • Each menu offers three or four versions of a word or phrase. Often the versions differ by a single letter (affect/effect), a capital letter (Fall/fall), or a punctuation mark (a comma moved one word over). Teach learners to read the whole sentence with each option plugged in.
  • Typical wording: “Select the option that correctly completes the sentence” or “Choose the correct word or phrase for each drop-down.”
  • The same conventions count on the extended response.
student:
Why this matters

On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, you will read short drafts such as emails, notices, and letters. Some sentences contain drop-down menus, and you choose the version that is correct. The choices may differ by just one letter, one capital, or one comma. The good news is that the same few rules come up over and over. This week you will learn those rules and a quick test for each one.

1. Subjects and verbs must agree

A singular subject needs a singular verb. A plural subject needs a plural verb.

  • The manager signs the forms. (one manager)
  • The managers sign the forms. (more than one)

Test: cross out the middle. Phrases like of the boxes, in the office, along with her team, and as well as never change the subject. Cross them out, then match the verb to what is left.

Words like each, every, everyone, nobody, and someone are singular. Two subjects joined by and are plural. With or or nor, match the verb to the subject closer to it.

Worked example 1. “The cost of the new uniforms (is / are) higher than last year.”

Step 1: Cross out “of the new uniforms.”

Step 2: What is left is “The cost (is / are) higher.” The subject is cost, which is singular.

Step 3: Answer: is. “Uniforms are” sounds natural only because uniforms sits next to the verb.

2. Pronouns: agreement and case

A pronoun must match the word it replaces. The workers brought their tools. The store changed its hours.

Pronouns also change form depending on their job in the sentence.

Doing the action (subject)Receiving the action or after a preposition (object)
I, he, she, we, theyme, him, her, us, them

Test: drop the partner. When a pronoun is paired with another person, cover the other person and read the sentence. “Ms. Bell called Jo and (I / me)” becomes “Ms. Bell called me.” So the answer is me.

Worked example 2. “My sister and (I / me) start classes in January.”

Step 1: Cover “My sister and.”

Step 2: Read both: “I start classes” or “Me start classes.”

Step 3: “I start” is correct. The pronoun is doing the action, so it is a subject. Answer: I.

Remember: between you and me is always correct, because between is a preposition.

3. Keep verb tense consistent

Look for time clues such as yesterday, last year, now, every day, and next week. Stay in the same tense unless the time really changes.

  • Wrong: Last week I called the office and ask for a refund.
  • Right: Last week I called the office and asked for a refund.

Use has or have with a past participle for something that started in the past and continues now: She has worked here since 2019.

4. Words that sound alike

WordsQuick test
their / there / they'reThey're = they are. Their = belongs to them. There = a place, or “there is/are.”
its / it'sIt's = it is or it has. Otherwise use its.
your / you'reYou're = you are. Otherwise use your.
affect / effectAffect is usually an action (to change something). Effect is usually a thing (a result). After a, an, the, use effect.
then / thanThan compares (more than, less than). Then tells when.

5. Capital letters

  • Capitalize specific names: people, cities, streets, businesses, days, months, holidays, and languages (Main Street, Friday, July, Thanksgiving, Spanish).
  • Do not capitalize seasons or general words: spring, fall, the street, a hospital, math.

6. Apostrophes

  • One owner: add 's (the driver's license).
  • More than one owner, word ends in -s: add just ' (the drivers' lounge).
  • Contractions: the apostrophe takes the place of missing letters (can't, it's, we're).
  • Never use an apostrophe just to make a plural: two tickets, not two ticket's.

7. Commas

  • After an introductory clause or phrase: When the bell rings, line up.
  • In a list of three or more: eggs, bread, and milk.
  • Before and, but, or, so when joining two complete sentences: I called, but no one answered.
  • Around extra information: Our manager, Luis Ortega, approved the plan.
  • Never between a subject and its verb.

Worked example 3. Choose the correct option: “Our manager[    ▾] approved the new schedule.” Options: , Luis Ortega, / , Luis Ortega / Luis Ortega,

Step 1: The words are the same in every option, so this is a comma question.

Step 2: “Luis Ortega” is extra information that renames “our manager.” Extra information needs a comma on both sides.

Step 3: Answer: “Our manager, Luis Ortega, approved the new schedule.” The other options use only one comma, which either splits the subject from its verb or leaves the extra information half-marked.

Strategy for drop-down menus: First, notice what is different among the options. If only the commas change, think comma rules. If only one letter changes, think confused words or agreement. Then read the whole sentence with each option before you choose.

Try it

1. Choose the verb: “The list of supplies (is / are) on the counter.”

Show answer

is. Cross out “of supplies.” The subject is list, which is singular.

2. Choose the pronoun: “Ms. Bell gave the keys to Ray and (I / me).”

Show answer

me. Drop “Ray and”: “gave the keys to me.” The pronoun comes after the preposition to, so it takes object case.

3. Choose both verbs: “Yesterday I (call / called) the landlord, and he (fixes / fixed) the sink an hour later.”

Show answer

called and fixed. “Yesterday” puts both actions in the past.

4. Fix the two errors: “Its time to check you're email.”

Show answer

“It's time to check your email.” It's means “it is.” Your shows that the email belongs to you; “check you are email” makes no sense.

5. Add the missing capital letters and commas: “after the meeting on tuesday we ordered paper, pens and folders.”

Show answer

“After the meeting on Tuesday, we ordered paper, pens, and folders.” Capitalize the first word and the day of the week. Put a comma after the introductory phrase and before and in the list. (Some style guides leave out the comma before and in a list, but including it is always correct.)
post:
Summary of key points

  • Agreement: Find the real subject by crossing out phrases in the middle. Singular subjects take singular verbs. Each, every, and everyone are singular. With or or nor, match the closer subject.
  • Pronouns: A pronoun matches the word it replaces (workers ... their; store ... its). Use the drop-the-partner test to choose between I and me, she and her.
  • Tense: Follow the time clues and do not switch tenses without a reason.
  • Confused words: Say the long form aloud: “it is,” “they are,” “you are.” Use than for comparisons and effect after a, an, or the.
  • Capitals: specific names, days, months, holidays, and languages, but not seasons or general words.
  • Apostrophes: for possession and contractions, never for plain plurals or possessive pronouns.
  • Commas: after introductory elements, in lists, before and/but/so joining two sentences, and around extra information. Never between a subject and its verb.

Exit ticket

1. Choose: “Everyone in the two classes (has / have) a locker.”

Show answer

has. Everyone is singular; “in the two classes” does not change the subject.

2. Choose: “The trainer showed Malik and (I / me) the new software.”

Show answer

me. “The trainer showed me” is correct; the pronoun receives the action.

3. Choose: “The new hours had a big (affect / effect) on sales.”

Show answer

effect. After “a big,” you need a noun meaning “result.”

4. Fix: “The team lost it's first game in the spring.”

Show answer

its first game. “Lost it is first game” makes no sense, so no apostrophe. “Spring” stays lowercase.

5. Add commas: “Our landlord Ms. Patel fixed the heater.” (Ms. Patel is the only landlord.)

Show answer

“Our landlord, Ms. Patel, fixed the heater.” The name is extra information about the one landlord, so it takes a pair of commas.

Reflection

  1. Which of this week's rules did you already use correctly without thinking? Which one surprised you?
  2. Look at a text message or email you wrote recently. Find one sentence you would change after this lesson, and explain why.
  3. Which quick test (cross out the middle, drop the partner, say the long form) will be most useful to you on test day?

This week's study plan (20–40 minutes a day)

  • Day 1: Reread sections 1 and 2 of the Student Lesson. Complete practice items 1–3. For each mistake, write the rule in your own words.
  • Day 2: Reread sections 3 and 4. Write five sentences of your own, each using one confused-word pair correctly. Complete practice items 4–6.
  • Day 3: Reread sections 5–7. Complete practice items 7–9. Make flash cards for the vocabulary terms.
  • Day 4: Complete practice items 10–12. Then edit one paragraph you wrote in an earlier week, checking agreement, tense, and commas.
  • Day 5: Take this week's Practice GED. Keep the Notes sheet out of sight until you finish.
  • Day 6: Review every Practice GED item you missed. Label each one with the rule it tested and rework it.
  • Day 7: Rest, or spend 20 minutes rereading the Notes sheet and the Week 7 sentence-structure rules.

Test-taking strategy: spot the difference first

When you open a drop-down menu, do not start by asking “Which one sounds right?” Instead, compare the options and find exactly what changes. If only a comma moves, apply a comma rule. If only a capital letter changes, ask whether the word is a specific name. If only one letter or one word changes, think agreement, tense, or confused words. Naming the rule before you choose keeps you from being fooled by an option that simply “sounds” familiar.

vocab.def: The word or words that tell who or what a sentence is about; the doer of the action.
The rule that a singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb.
A group of words that begins with a word such as of, in, on, with, or for. It never contains the subject of the sentence.
A pronoun that does not name a specific person or thing, such as each, everyone, someone, or nobody. Most are singular.
The word a pronoun replaces or refers to.
vocab.example: The company changed its hours. (company is the antecedent of its)

vocab.def: The form a pronoun takes depending on its job: subject case (I, she, we) or object case (me, her, us).
The form of a verb that shows when an action happens: past, present, or future.
A verb form made with has or have plus a past participle, used for an action that began in the past and continues or still matters now.
Words that sound alike but have different spellings and meanings.
A shortened word in which an apostrophe replaces missing letters.
vocab.example: it's = it is; they're = they are

vocab.def: A form that shows ownership, usually with an apostrophe for nouns. Possessive pronouns (its, theirs, yours) never use one.
The name of a specific person, place, organization, or thing. It is always capitalized.
A word, phrase, or clause that comes before the main part of a sentence. It is usually followed by a comma.
Extra information that can be removed without changing the basic meaning of the sentence. It is set off with a pair of commas.
vocab.example: Our supervisor, Dana Whitfield, is on site.

notes:
Week 8 RLA Study Sheet: Grammar II

Subject-verb agreement

  • Cross out phrases in the middle (of, in, with, along with, as well as).
  • each, every, everyone, nobody, someone = singular
  • A and B = plural
  • A or/nor B = match the closer one
  • There is (one) / There are (many)
  • A company, team, or committee = singular

Pronouns

SubjectObject
I, he, she, we, they, whome, him, her, us, them, whom
  • Drop the partner: Jo and (I/me)
  • between you and me
  • Plural antecedent → their; a thing → its

Verb tense

  • Follow time clues; do not switch without a reason.
  • has/have + participle: past that continues now (since, for).

Confused words

WordMeans
they're / it's / you'rethey are / it is / you are
their / its / yourbelongs to
thereplace; there is/are
affect / effectto influence / a result
than / thencompare / time

Capitals

YES: names, streets, cities, days, months, holidays, languages, title + name. NO: seasons, general words, most school subjects.

Apostrophes

  • one owner: 's; plural owners ending in -s: s'
  • contractions: don't, it's
  • NEVER for plain plurals or its, yours, theirs

Commas

  • after an introductory element
  • items in a series (3+)
  • before and/but/or/so joining two sentences
  • a pair around extra information
  • NEVER between subject and verb

Drop-down routine: (1) Spot what changes among the options. (2) Name the rule. (3) Read the whole sentence with each option. (4) Choose.

stimuli.title: Draft Email: New Check-In Tablets
stimuli.source: Original document written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
The following email is a first draft. Lettered blanks mark places where you will choose the correct word. Some other sentences contain errors that the questions ask about.

To: Front Desk and Clinical Staff
From: Maribel Ortiz, Office Manager
Subject: New check-in tablets start Monday

Hi everyone,

(1) Starting Monday, our front desk will replace the paper sign-in sheet with two check-in tablets. The tablets sends each patient's information directly to our scheduling system, so we will no longer need to type it in by hand. This change should shorten the line at the desk during our busiest hours.

(2) Patients will still need to show (A) insurance cards to the receptionist, who will scan them as usual. The tablets are sturdy, but they are not waterproof. Please wipe down each tablet and (B) case after every patient, using the gray cloths in the top drawer rather than spray cleaner.

(3) We tested the tablets for two weeks at our Eastside office. Check-in took about four minutes less per patient then it did with paper forms, and the staff there reported fewer mistakes in phone numbers and addresses.

(4) I will hold a short training in the break room on Friday at 12:30. Please bring any questions you have. Thank you for helping our patients get settled faster.

Maribel

TOWN OF LARKSPUR, DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS
Notice to Residents: Water Main Replacement

(1) The town will replace the water main under (A) between Elm Avenue and Fourth Street. The current pipe was installed in 1958 and has broken three times in the past two years. Crews will begin work the week after Labor Day, and the project should be complete by late (B).

(2) Residents who park on the street should move his or her vehicles to the lot behind Larkspur Elementary School before 7:00 a.m. on weekdays. Driveways will remain open except for a few hours on the day crews dig in front of each home.

(3) (C) please fill several containers with drinking water the night before. You will receive a door hanger at least one day before your service is shut off. During the work, you may also notice (D)

(4) We thank you for your patience. Questions may be directed to the Public Works office at Town Hall, 22 Main Street, Monday through Friday.

stimuli.title: Draft Letter: Job Application
stimuli.source: Original document written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
The following cover letter is a first draft. Lettered blanks mark places where you will choose the correct option. Some other sentences contain errors that the questions ask about.

Dear Ms. Grant:

(1) I am writing to apply for the assistant manager position at Cedar Grove Market that was posted on your website. (A) clear from your job posting that you need someone who can train new staff and keep a busy store running smoothly. I believe my four years at Bayside Foods have prepared me to do both.

(2) At Bayside, I started as a cashier and was promoted to shift supervisor in my second year. Last year, I trained six new cashiers and create a checklist that cut our opening time by fifteen minutes. I also planned the (B) schedules for the holiday season, making sure that all twelve cashiers had at least one weekend day off.

(3) Good scheduling had a positive (C) on our team. During the holidays, sick calls dropped, and customers noticed shorter lines. My store manager, Ms. Reyes, has offered to speak with you about the work her and me did together on the holiday schedule.

(4) Thank you for considering my application. I would welcome the chance to meet with you, and I can be reached at the phone number listed on my résumé.

Sincerely,
Andre Mitchell

The following neighborhood newsletter article is a first draft. Some sentences contain errors that the questions ask about.

(1) Do you have a lamp that flickers or a jacket with a broken zipper? Bring it to the Repair Café, where volunteers fix household items for free.

(2) The Repair Café meets on the second Saturday of every month in the community center's back room. Volunteers fix lamps, toasters, bicycles, and clothing at no charge. Last month's total was a record: forty-one items repaired. The volunteers answer visitors' questions as they work, so many people learn to make simple repairs themselves. We are always looking for volunteer's who can sew. If you can thread a needle, we can teach you the rest.

(3) The café does not charge for repairs, and it does not accept tips. Neither the organizers nor the center's director expect the event to make money. The goal is to keep useful items out of the landfill and to help neighbors meet one another.

(4) On saturday, march 14, the Repair Café will hold it's first spring event at Lincoln Park. Volunteers will set up tables near the playground from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 1 of the email.

“The tablets sends each patient's information directly to our scheduling system, so we will no longer need to type it in by hand.”

Which is the correct way to write the underlined word?
items.hint: Find the subject of the verb. Is it one tablet or more than one?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the subject: The tablets. It ends in -s and the email says there are two tablets, so the subject is plural.

Step 2. A plural subject needs a plural verb. In the present tense, the plural form has no -s: The tablets send.

Step 3. Check the tense. The rest of the email describes how the system will work from now on in the present and future (“we will no longer need”), so present tense fits.

Why the others are wrong: sends, is sending, and has sent are all singular forms (they go with it or the tablet), so none of them agrees with tablets. Has sent would also wrongly suggest an action already completed.

items.prompt:
Read the email. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Paragraph 2, blank (A): “Patients will still need to show {{0}} insurance cards to the receptionist, who will scan them as usual.”

Paragraph 2, blank (B): “Please wipe down each tablet and {{1}} case after every patient, using the gray cloths in the top drawer rather than spray cleaner.”
items.hint: Try replacing each choice with its long form: “they are” or “it is.” If the long form makes no sense, it is not the contraction.
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: The cards belong to the patients, so the word must show ownership. Step 2: Test they're: “show they are insurance cards” makes no sense. Step 3: There points to a place or begins “there is/are”; it does not show ownership. Step 4: Their means “belonging to them.” Answer: their insurance cards.

Blank (B). Step 1: The case belongs to the tablet, so the word must show ownership. Step 2: Test it's: “each tablet and it is case” makes no sense, so it's is wrong. Step 3: Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe, and its' is not a word. Answer: its case.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 3 of the email.

“Check-in took about four minutes less per patient then it did with paper forms, and the staff there reported fewer mistakes in phone numbers and addresses.”

Which is the correct way to write the underlined word?
items.hint: Is the sentence telling when something happened, or comparing two things?
items.explain:
Step 1. Decide what the sentence is doing. It compares the time check-in takes with tablets to the time it took with paper forms.

Step 2. Comparisons use than, especially after words like less, more, fewer, and rather: “four minutes less per patient than it did with paper forms.”

Why the others are wrong: Then refers to time or a next step (“first this, then that”), so it does not make a comparison. That and as do not complete a comparison that begins with less; “less ... as” and “less ... that it did” are not standard English.

items.prompt:
Read the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Paragraph 1, blank (A): “The town will replace the water main under {{0}} between Elm Avenue and Fourth Street.”

Paragraph 1, blank (B): “Crews will begin work the week after Labor Day, and the project should be complete by late {{1}}.”
items.hint: Only the capital letters change. Ask of each word: is it the name of one specific place or holiday, or is it a general word?
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: The options differ only in capital letters. Step 2: “Juniper Street” is the full name of one specific street, so it is a proper noun. Step 3: Both words in a street name are capitalized, just like “Elm Avenue” and “Fourth Street” in the same sentence. Answer: Juniper Street.

Blank (B). Step 1: Check each word. Step 2: Seasons (fall, spring, summer, winter) are general words and are not capitalized, so “Fall” is wrong in the middle of a sentence. Step 3: Holidays are proper nouns and are capitalized, like “Labor Day” earlier in the sentence. Answer: fall, before Thanksgiving. The other options either capitalize the season or leave the holiday lowercase.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 2 of the notice.

“Residents who park on the street should move his or her vehicles to the lot behind Larkspur Elementary School before 7:00 a.m. on weekdays.”

Which is the correct way to write the underlined portion?
items.hint: Which word does the pronoun refer back to? Is that word singular or plural?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the antecedent, the word the pronoun refers to. The vehicles belong to the Residents.

Step 2. Residents is plural, so the pronoun must be plural: their.

Step 3. Check spelling: the possessive form is their (belonging to them). Answer: “Residents ... should move their vehicles.”

Why the others are wrong: His or her is singular, so it does not match a plural antecedent. Its is singular and refers to things, not people. There is a place word, not a possessive, so it is a confused-word error.

items.prompt:
Read the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Paragraph 3, blank (C): “{{0}} please fill several containers with drinking water the night before.”

Paragraph 3, blank (D): “During the work, you may also notice {{1}}”

options: Because water service to each home will be off for up to six hours,
Because water service to each home will be off for up to six hours
Because, water service to each home will be off for up to six hours,
Because water service to each home, will be off for up to six hours,
noise, dust, and short traffic delays.
noise dust and short traffic delays.
noise, dust and, short traffic delays.
noise, dust, and, short traffic delays.

items.hint: The words are the same in every option, so this is about commas. For (C), where does the introductory part end? For (D), how many items are in the list?
items.explain:
Blank (C). Step 1: “Because water service to each home will be off for up to six hours” is an introductory clause: it has a subject (water service) and a verb (will be), and it comes before the main part of the sentence (please fill ...). Step 2: An introductory clause is followed by a comma, so the option with no comma is wrong. Step 3: No comma belongs right after Because, and no comma belongs between the subject water service to each home and its verb will be. Answer: the version with a single comma after hours, at the end of the clause.

Blank (D). Step 1: The list has three items: noise, dust, and short traffic delays. Step 2: Items in a series of three or more are separated by commas, with and before the last item: “noise, dust, and short traffic delays.” Step 3: The other options either leave out the commas entirely or put a comma after and, which wrongly separates and from the item it introduces. (Some styles drop the comma before and, but that version is not offered here, and the version with it is always correct.)

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 2 of the letter.

“Last year, I trained six new cashiers and create a checklist that cut our opening time by fifteen minutes.”

Which is the correct way to write the underlined word?
items.hint: Look at the time clue at the start of the sentence and at the other verbs in it.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the time clue: “Last year” places the action in the past.

Step 2. Look at the other verbs. Trained and cut are both past tense, and create is joined to trained by and, so the two verbs should match.

Step 3. The past tense of create is created: “I trained six new cashiers and created a checklist.”

Why the others are wrong: Create and am creating are present tense, and will create is future tense. All three shift away from the past for no reason, which is a tense-consistency error.

items.prompt: Read paragraph 2 of the newsletter article. Click the sentence that contains an error in the use of an apostrophe.
spans: The Repair Café meets on the second Saturday of every month in the community center's back room.
Volunteers fix lamps, toasters, bicycles, and clothing at no charge.
Last month's total was a record: forty-one items repaired.
The volunteers answer visitors' questions as they work, so many people learn to make simple repairs themselves.
We are always looking for volunteer's who can sew.
If you can thread a needle, we can teach you the rest.
items.hint: For each apostrophe, ask: is this word showing ownership or a contraction? If it is only a plural, it should not have an apostrophe.
items.explain:
Step 1. Check every apostrophe in the paragraph.

  • center's back room: the back room belongs to one center. Correct.
  • Last month's total: the total belongs to last month. Correct.
  • visitors' questions: the questions belong to many visitors, so the apostrophe goes after the -s. Correct.
  • volunteer's who can sew: nothing belongs to the volunteers here. The writer simply means more than one volunteer. Error.

Step 2. The sentence “We are always looking for volunteer's who can sew” uses an apostrophe to make a plural. It should read “We are always looking for volunteers who can sew.”

Step 3. The remaining sentences have no apostrophes and no errors. A common trap is choosing “visitors' questions” because the apostrophe comes after the -s, but that is the correct form for a plural owner.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 3 of the letter.

“My store manager, Ms. Reyes, has offered to speak with you about the work her and me did together on the holiday schedule.”

Which is the correct way to write the underlined portion?
items.hint: The two pronouns are the ones who “did” the work. Test each pronoun alone with the verb “did.”
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the job of the pronouns. In the clause “(that) ___ and ___ did together,” the pronouns are the ones doing the action did. That makes them subjects.

Step 2. Subjects take subject case: I, he, she, we, they.

Step 3. Drop the partner to check each one: “the work she did” (not “her did”) and “the work I did” (not “me did”).

Step 4. Answer: “the work she and I did together.”

Why the others are wrong: “Her and me” uses object case for both. “Her and I” and “she and me” each get only one pronoun right. The trap is that the clause comes right after the preposition about, but the object of about is the work, not the pronouns.

items.prompt:
Read the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Paragraph 1, blank (A): “{{0}} clear from your job posting that you need someone who can train new staff and keep a busy store running smoothly.”

Paragraph 2, blank (B): “I also planned the {{1}} schedules for the holiday season, making sure that all twelve cashiers had at least one weekend day off.”

Paragraph 3, blank (C): “Good scheduling had a positive {{2}} on our team.”
items.hint: For (A), try “It is.” For (B), count the owners: how many cashiers have schedules? For (C), look at the word “a” before the blank.
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: Read it as “It is clear from your job posting.” That makes sense, so the contraction It's is correct. Step 2: Its shows possession (“Its clear” would mean “the clear belonging to it”), and Its' is not a word. Answer: It's.

Blank (B). Step 1: The schedules belong to the cashiers, so a possessive is needed. Step 2: The sentence says there are twelve cashiers, so the owner is plural. Step 3: For a plural noun ending in -s, add only an apostrophe: cashiers'. Step 4: Cashier's means one cashier; cashiers has no apostrophe to show ownership; cashiers's adds an extra -s that plural possessives do not take.

Blank (C). Step 1: The blank follows “a positive,” so it must be a noun (a thing), and a singular one because of a. Step 2: Effect is the noun meaning “result.” Answer: “a positive effect on our team.” Step 3: Affect and affects are verbs, and effects is plural, which does not fit after a.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 3 of the newsletter article.

“Neither the organizers nor the center's director expect the event to make money.”

Which is the correct way to write the underlined word?
items.hint: When two subjects are joined by “neither ... nor,” the verb agrees with the subject that is closer to it.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the subjects: the organizers and the center's director, joined by neither ... nor.

Step 2. With or or nor, the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. The closer subject is the center's director, which is singular.

Step 3. The paragraph is in the present tense (“does not charge,” “The goal is”), so use the singular present form: “Neither the organizers nor the center's director expects the event to make money.”

Why the others are wrong: Expect, are expecting, and have expected are all plural forms. They would agree with organizers, but that subject is farther from the verb. Treating two subjects as automatically plural works with and, not with nor.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 4 of the newsletter article.

“On saturday, march 14, the Repair Café will hold it's first spring event at Lincoln Park.”

Which revision of the sentence corrects all of its errors?
options: On Saturday, March 14, the Repair Café will hold its first spring event at Lincoln Park.
On Saturday, March 14, the Repair Café will hold it's first Spring event at Lincoln Park.
On saturday, March 14, the Repair Café will hold its first spring event at Lincoln park.
On Saturday, March 14, the Repair Café will hold its first Spring event at Lincoln park.
items.hint: Check each word that could be capitalized: is it a specific name, day, or month, or is it a season or general word? Then test “it's” by reading it as “it is.”
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the errors in the original. saturday is a day of the week and march is a month, so both must be capitalized. It's means “it is,” and “will hold it is first spring event” makes no sense, so the possessive its is needed.

Step 2. Check the words that are already correct. spring is a season, so it stays lowercase. Lincoln Park is the name of a specific park, so both words stay capitalized. Repair Café is the name of the group, so it stays capitalized.

Step 3. Only one revision fixes all three errors and keeps every correct word: “On Saturday, March 14, the Repair Café will hold its first spring event at Lincoln Park.”

Why the others are wrong: One revision keeps it's and wrongly capitalizes Spring. Another leaves saturday lowercase and lowercases park in a proper name. The remaining one capitalizes Spring and lowercases park.
